result: Background information on Rab proteins, Mical family, and EHBP family is provided, establishing the context for the study. These claims describe the known roles of Rab proteins in vesicular trafficking, their regulation by GEFs and GAPs, their interaction with effector proteins, and the domain architecture of Mical and EHBP proteins including the DUF3585/bMERB domain.
evaluation: Claims C1-C21 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Takai et al., 2001; Stenmark, 2009; Grosshans et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2005; Giridharan and Caplan, 2014; Shi et al., 2010; etc.) or reference to established databases (SMART). These are background claims establishing the scientific context and are appropriately documented.

result: The bMERB domains preferentially bind Rab8 family members (Rab8, Rab10, Rab13, Rab15) with high nanomolar affinities (33-790 nM), while showing weak or no binding to Rab1 (KD 2.2-5.2 µM for Mical proteins, no detectable binding for EHBPs). This specificity was demonstrated through aSEC and ITC experiments.
evaluation: Claims C22-C31 are well-supported by systematic experimental data from aSEC (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and ITC measurements (Table 1, Figures 2a-b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The experiments were performed with appropriate controls, technical replicates, and the data consistently show the preferential binding to Rab8 family members over Rab1.

result: Some bMERB domains (Mical-1, Mical-3, EHBP1L1) can bind two Rab8 molecules simultaneously in a 2:1 stoichiometry, while others (Mical-cL, EHBP1) bind in a 1:1 stoichiometry. Mical-1 and EHBP1L1 contain two high-affinity binding sites, while Mical-3 contains one high-affinity and one lower-affinity site.
evaluation: Claims C32-C39 are supported by converging evidence from ITC experiments showing 2:1 stoichiometry (Table 1, Figure 2b) and aSEC experiments with varying protein ratios confirming the stoichiometry differences (Figure 2c). The characterization of binding site affinities is based on thermodynamic parameters from ITC data.

result: bMERB domains can simultaneously bind two different Rab proteins (Rab8 and Rab13) in a 1:1:1 ternary complex, as demonstrated by aSEC experiments for Mical-1 and EHBP1L1.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by aSEC experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) showing formation of ternary complexes. C40 is additionally supported by citation to prior work (Sun et al., 2010, 2016) showing functional relevance of Rab8/Rab13 cooperation.

result: EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 can be prenylated in vitro (preferentially farnesylated), and this prenylation is necessary for their localization to endosomal structures where they colocalize with constitutively active Rab8 and Rab10.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by mass spectrometry data showing prenylation (Figure 3a), fluorescence microscopy showing CaaX-dependent localization (Figure 3b), and colocalization with active Rab8/Rab10 (Figure 3c). The preferential farnesylation is consistent with the CaaX-box sequences and cited literature (Zhang and Casey, 1996).

result: The crystal structure of Mical-3 bMERB domain was solved at 2.7 Å resolution, revealing a dimeric structure with each monomer consisting of three α-helices forming a central 4-stranded coiled-coil.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by X-ray crystallography data with appropriate statistics (Table 2) and structural analysis (Figure 4a). The resolution is adequate for the structural conclusions drawn, and refinement statistics are within acceptable ranges.

result: Crystal structures of Rab1, Rab8, and Rab10 in complex with Mical-cL show 1:1 stoichiometry with interactions primarily involving α-helix 3 of Mical-cL and the switch regions of Rabs. The Rab-binding interface overlaps with the dimer interface observed in Mical-3, and Rab binding disrupts the dimer in Mical-3 and Mical-cL.
evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by multiple crystal structures (Table 2, Figure 5a) and aSEC data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The structural analysis is detailed and consistent with known Rab:effector interactions. The observation about dimer disruption is supported by aSEC experiments showing different elution profiles.

result: The specificity of bMERB domains for Rab8 family members is determined by interactions with RabSF1 and RabSF2 motifs, and critically, by N-terminal residues preceding RabSF1. Rab1 contains Glu4 while Rab8 family members contain Lys residues that interact with a negatively charged patch in Mical-cL. A Rab1 chimera with the N-terminus of Rab8 (Rab1R8N) showed ~5-fold increased affinity and gained the ability to bind EHBPs.
evaluation: Claims C53-C62 are strongly supported by structural analysis (Figure 5), sequence alignments showing conservation patterns, crystal structure of Rab1R8N:Mical-cL (Figure 5a), ITC data showing increased affinity (Figure 5c), and aSEC experiments showing gained binding to EHBPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b). The chimera experiment provides compelling evidence for the role of N-terminal residues in specificity.

result: The crystal structure of Mical-1 in complex with Rab10 reveals two separate Rab binding sites within a single bMERB domain: an N-terminal site (α-helix 1 and first half of α-helix 2) and a C-terminal site (second half of α-helix 2 and α-helix 3). Both sites show strong structural similarity and use similar interacting residues. Deletion experiments confirm that each site independently binds Rab, with the C-terminal site having higher affinity.
evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by the crystal structure at 2.8 Å resolution (Figure 6a, Table 2), detailed structural analysis showing similarity between sites, and deletion experiments using both aSEC and ITC (Figure 6c) that confirm the independent function of each site and their different affinities.

result: The two Rab binding sites in bMERB domains evolved via gene duplication of a common ancestor α-hairpin motif. The strong conservation of interacting residues between both sites within Mical-1 and across different bMERB domains suggests all these proteins contain two binding sites (though the second may be low affinity in some cases). The architecture resembles spectrin repeats with a continuous connecting helix.
evaluation: Claims C69-C104 are supported by structural analysis showing similarity between binding sites (Figure 6a), sequence alignments showing conservation patterns (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3), and comparison with known structures (citations to Khan and Ménétrey, 2013; Eathiraj et al., 2005; Han et al., 2007; Pascual et al., 1997). The evolutionary inference is reasonable given the structural and sequence evidence, though it remains an inference rather than direct experimental proof.

result: The bMERB domains constitute a Rab8-effector family involved in endosomal trafficking. The Rab-binding specificity can be explained by the 3D structures, with specificity-determining interactions involving RabSF1, RabSF2, and notably the N-terminal residues preceding RabSF1—a novel specificity determinant not previously observed in other Rab:effector interactions.
evaluation: Claims C71-C78 are well-supported by the comprehensive structural and biochemical data presented in the study. The identification of N-terminal residues as specificity determinants is a novel finding supported by structural analysis and the Rab1R8N chimera experiments. The claim about novelty (C78) is reasonable given the comparison with existing literature.

result: The bMERB domains show structural similarity to other Rab effector proteins, particularly in the positioning of the main interacting helix and conservation of key residues (Arg/Lys contacting Asp45, Asp/Asn contacting Gln61). The binding affinities are similar to those of Rab27:Slp2-a and Rab27:Slac2a, which are among the highest observed for Rab:effector interactions.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by structural comparisons with cited structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and affinity data from literature (Fukuda, 2006). The structural similarities are clearly demonstrated, and the affinity comparisons are appropriately referenced.

result: This work constitutes the first description of two Rab proteins binding a single effector domain. While multivalent Rab effectors have been described previously (Rabaptin-5, Rab6IP1, Gcc185), all previously described effectors contain separate Rab-binding domains that each bind only one Rab protein.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Oesterlin et al., 2014; Vitale et al., 1998; Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007; Hayes et al., 2009) and the novel structural and biochemical data from this study. The claim of novelty appears justified based on the comparison with existing literature.

result: The authors propose several potential functions for bivalent bMERB domains: linking vesicles to target membranes, acting in positive feedback loops to establish Rab microdomains, functioning as Rab hubs to connect different trafficking pathways, and having separate functions for the two binding sites (membrane recruitment vs. auto-inhibition release). These proposals are supported by prior work on Mical-L1 and Mical-L2.
evaluation: Claims C88-C98 are largely speculative (as indicated by evidence_type SPECULATION for many claims) or based on prior work by others (C89, C93, C94, C97). While the speculation is reasonable and grounded in the structural findings and cited literature (Pfeffer, 2013; Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007; Rahajeng et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2010, 2016; Kobayashi et al., 2014), these functional hypotheses are not directly tested in this study. The structural basis for these functions is established (C95), but the actual biological functions remain to be experimentally validated.
